topic.label: EEG & Signal Methods
topic.description: EEG signal processing, sleep staging, neural time series, modeling, and practical analysis methods.

papers.title: Somnus, a tunable, open-source platform for automated EEG sleep scoring in physiological and disease mouse models
papers.abstract: Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG. The features that researchers measure in these recordings, such as seizures and epileptiform activity, are deeply influenced by whether the animal is awake, in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, or in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Because total sleep duration varies naturally across animals, rigorous experimental comparisons require classifying the sleep state of every few seconds of a recording. Manual annotation is highly labor-intensive, often requiring hours per subject. While automated scoring tools accelerate this process, they are typically trained exclusively on healthy cohorts and frequently fail when applied to disease models that exhibit atypical or fragmented sleep architecture. Somnus is an open-source Python package designed to automate rodent sleep staging using EEG, muscle activity (EMG), and optional video-tracking data. It includes a robust base model trained on diverse recordings from six independent laboratories, enabling out-of-the-box classification across various equipment setups without requiring prior manual labeling. A central feature of Somnus is its capacity for rapid adaptation to pathological sleep structure. The software provides a graphical interface that directs researchers to the specific epochs where the base model is least certain. Users can manually correct these targeted epochs in a built-in viewer by comparing the model's classification to the raw EEG signal and video, and then use their corrections to fine-tune the model. This workflow empowers researchers to generate accurate custom scorers for complex disease models or novel treatments with just a few minutes of manual correction, bypassing the need to hand-score entire experimental cohorts or develop their own models from scratch.

ai.reason: Directly addresses core needs with a tunable open-source Python platform for mouse EEG/EMG sleep scoring that generalizes across labs and disease models without retraining.
ai.summary: Somnus is an open-source Python platform for automated sleep staging in rodents using EEG, EMG, and optional video. Its base model, trained across diverse recordings from six laboratories, enables rapid fine-tuning via a graphical interface that targets uncertain epochs, allowing accurate custom scorers for disease models with minimal manual correction.

papers.title: What EEG doesn't see: a whole-brain MEG map of sleep spindles and slow oscillations
papers.abstract: Sleep spindles and slow oscillations (SOs) are hallmarks of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, linked to memory consolidation and restorative functions. They are usually detected in one or a few scalp electroencephalography (EEG) channels with parameters that vary across studies, and serve as the reference even in magnetoencephalography (MEG), fMRI and intracranial studies. We argue that these choices filter which neural activity is captured. Nineteen young adults took a daytime nap during simultaneous MEG and EEG. Using MEG source imaging across 416 cortical, subcortical and cerebellar regions, we mapped the amplitude and density of SOs (0.5-4 Hz, and 0.5-2 and 2-4 Hz separately) and of spindles (9-18 Hz, and slow, 9-12.9 Hz, and fast, 13-18 Hz, separately), and related each region's activity to a single scalp derivation (Cz-M1). Both rhythms were detected throughout the brain, including the thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala, basal ganglia and cerebellum. The balance between bands varied across regions: fast spindles predominated over slow spindles along the dorsal midline, around the central sulcus and in the thalamus, slow spindles predominated in occipital cortex and the cerebellar hemispheres, and 2-4 Hz SOs were relatively most prominent in occipital cortex. Amplitude and density formed reliable but distinct maps: regions with larger fast spindles also had more of them, whereas SOs, and slow spindles once source depth was controlled, were larger where they were less frequent. More SOs were detected in every region than at Cz-M1, whereas more fast spindles were detected at Cz-M1 than in any single region. Around the SO, slow-spindle activity had the same timing at the scalp and in the sources, but the up-state increase in fast-spindle activity seen at the scalp was absent from local sources. Slow spindles were the most strongly shared events, and sensorimotor sources the most scalp-like. Thus, a single scalp derivation offers a selective and partly composite view of sleep oscillations, with implications for interpreting their functional roles and for targeting them with closed-loop auditory stimulation

ai.topic: MEG/EEG sleep spindle and slow oscillation mapping
ai.reason: Directly addresses sleep spindle/SO detection and the limitations of single-channel EEG derivations, with strong implications for animal sleep analysis, signal normalization, and multi-region vigilance-state methods.
ai.summary: Simultaneous MEG/EEG during daytime naps in 19 young adults showed that sleep spindles and slow oscillations occur throughout the brain, including thalamus, hippocampus, and cerebellum, with region-specific balances between fast/slow spindles and SO frequency bands. A single scalp derivation (Cz-M1) provides a selective and partly composite view: more SOs were detected in every brain region than at Cz-M1, whereas fast spindles were more frequent at Cz-M1 than in any single source region.

papers.title: Predicting ICU Seizures Using 1 hour of cEEG.
papers.abstract: Continuous electroencephalography (cEEG) is the gold standard for detecting electrographic seizures in the intensive care unit (ICU), but limited resources limit prolonged monitoring for all patients. We developed an automated, interpretable pipeline that uses a single hour of cEEG to estimate near-term seizure risk across multiple prediction windows. We retrospectively studied 50 adults who underwent ICU cEEG monitoring at a single tertiary center. From a 1-hour segment, we computed automated interictal-ictal continuum (IIC) burden probabilities for lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs), generalized periodic discharges (GPDs), and lateralized rhythmic delta activity (LRDA), along with quantitative background EEG features reflecting signal organization and hemispheric asymmetry. Segments were labeled by seizure occurrence within the subsequent 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, or 24 hours. Support vector machine (SVM) and bagged-tree classifiers were trained using clinical-only, background-only, and combined feature sets with a 70/30 patient-level train-test split and cross-validation within the training set. For the 4-hour horizon, the combined-feature SVM achieved 76% accuracy and the lowest Brier score (0.25), outperforming clinical-only (72%) and background-only (70%) models. Across horizons, SVM accuracy declined from 94% (1 hour) to 79% (24 hours) with increasing Brier scores, indicating reduced calibration at longer intervals. AUC-receiver operating characteristic increased with wider prediction windows, consistent with higher seizure prevalence at longer lead times. Integrating automated IIC probabilities with quantitative background EEG features enables moderate, interpretable near-term seizure prediction from a single hour of ICU cEEG. Initial external validation on an independent multicenter ICU cohort supports generalizability, although broader prospective and multicenter evaluation are needed before clinical deployment.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society

ai.reason: Automated, interpretable pipeline using lightweight SVM/tree classifiers on short EEG windows with strong transferable feature engineering for state/event prediction; aligns with CPU-friendly, small-data EEG classification goals.
ai.summary: An automated interpretable pipeline using one hour of ICU cEEG estimated near-term seizure risk from interictal-ictal continuum probabilities and quantitative background features in 50 adults. For the 4-hour horizon, a combined-feature SVM achieved 76% accuracy and Brier score 0.25, and accuracy declined from 94% at 1 hour to 79% at 24 hours, with initial external validation supporting generalizability.

papers.title: Distinct electroencephalography alpha-band rhythms map macroscale brain gradients.
papers.abstract: Brain gradients provide a low-dimensional framework for describing cortical organization, linking functional connectivity, anatomy, development, and transcriptional architecture. Whether this macroscale organization also structures fast electrophysiological dynamics remains less clear. Here we used the longstanding observation that alpha-band activity is not unitary, and that some individuals exhibit multiple alpha peaks, as an entry point for examining cortical gradients in resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). We analyzed source-reconstructed EEG from 608 adults, comprising 3,255 recordings acquired across eyes-open and eyes-closed rest before and after cognitive testing. Within individuals, parcel-wise alpha peak frequencies frequently departed from unimodality, revealing 2 separable alpha-frequency components in 38.3% of recordings. These components were not spatially arbitrary: frequency-defined clusters aligned with canonical functional networks, most prominently separating visual and somatomotor systems, although their relative frequency ordering varied across individuals. Low-dimensional analysis of cluster network composition further identified 2 principal axes: a sensory-differentiation axis contrasting visual and somatomotor contributions, and a sensorimotor-association axis resembling established functional-connectomic gradients. These findings suggest that split alpha reflects multiple sensory-anchored oscillatory modes embedded within macroscale cortical gradients, linking a classical EEG phenomenon to the brain's hierarchical architecture.

ai.reason: Spectral EEG analysis of alpha peaks and low-dimensional brain organization across 608 subjects; highly relevant to spectral/time-frequency methods and manifold-like dimensionality reduction, though less focused on animal sleep.
ai.summary: Using source-reconstructed resting-state EEG from 608 adults (3,255 recordings), the study found that 38.3% of recordings had separable alpha-frequency components that aligned with canonical functional networks, especially separating visual and somatomotor systems. Low-dimensional analysis identified a sensory-differentiation axis and a sensorimotor-association axis resembling functional-connectomic gradients, linking split alpha to macroscale cortical organization.

papers.title: EEG Pathology Detection via Clinical Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.abstract: Deep learning models for electroencephalography (EEG) pathology detection achieve competitive accuracy but offer limited interpretability. In this paper, we introduce concept bottleneck models (CBMs) for EEG pathology detection which use clinical EEG biomarkers computed analytically from the signal as a bottleneck to be used for prediction. Those concepts include band power, spectral ratios, alpha peak frequency and amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry and phase locking values. With the backbone based on shallow convolutional neural network (CNN), we compare a black box baseline with two variants of CBMs. The hybrid variant is a classifier receives a residual projection of the backbone features. The pure variant is a CBM where the classifier receives only the predicted concepts. Models are evaluated on abnormality detection and dementia classification followed by concept prediction quality and leakage analysis. Both CBMs approach the baseline on TUAB (82.7-82.9% vs 83.6%) and are 2-5 percentage points lower on CAUEEG (57.9-60.5% vs 62.7%). The pure CBM exhibits concept fidelity concern where the predicted concepts deviate from their ground truth values. Replacing them with their true values causes severe cost on accuracy by 26 and 22 points on TUAB and CAUEEG. The concept fidelity concern is mitigated by increasing the weight of the concept loss to match the ground truth concepts. the mitigation comes with small accuracy cost on TUAB but a relatively larger cost on CAUEEG. The code of the experiments and full logs are available at https://www.github.com/mhmdrdwn/cbm.

ai.topic: Interpretable EEG pathology detection via concept bottlenecks
ai.reason: Uses clinically interpretable spectral concepts and shallow CNNs for EEG classification, aligning with interpretable feature extraction and lightweight model priorities.
ai.summary: This study introduces concept bottleneck models for EEG pathology detection that use analytically computed clinical EEG biomarkers (e.g., band power, spectral ratios, phase locking values) as an interpretable bottleneck. The models approach black-box baseline accuracy on TUAB (82.7-82.9% vs 83.6%) but show lower performance on CAUEEG (57.9-60.5% vs 62.7%), with a pure CBM variant exhibiting concept fidelity concerns mitigated by increasing concept loss weight.

papers.title: Fixed-Sequence OFF-to-ON Differences in Low-Beta State Dynamics in Parkinson's Disease: A Paired Source-Space Resting-State EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Resting-state EEG studies in Parkinson's disease (PD) have largely emphasized static power or connectivity, whereas fixed-sequence OFF-to-ON session differences may also involve the temporal organization of network states. Paired source-space evidence under such fixed acquisition protocols remains limited. We analyzed 64-channel eyes-closed resting-state EEG in 39 patients with PD contributing paired OFF/ON recordings for the prespecified 90 s primary analysis; 24 also contributed paired 178 s recordings for duration robustness. After individual MRI-based source reconstruction, low-beta (13-20 Hz) dynamic amplitude-envelope connectivity was computed with 2 s windows. Primary endpoints were switching rate (SR) and normalized Shannon entropy (H); fractional occupancy (FO_path) and mean dwell time (MDT_path) of an internally defined OFF-dominant state were prespecified secondary conditional endpoints and are interpreted only as conditional summaries. PD-only linear mixed-effects models quantified the fixed-sequence OFF-to-ON session contrast; medication state and session order were necessarily collinear. In the 90 s analysis, the later ON session showed higher SR (β = 3.3224, Holm p = 0.00406) and H (β = 0.06781, Holm p = 0.000749) than the earlier OFF session. FO_path (β = -0.09167, Holm p = 1.08 × 10⁻⁵) and MDT_path (β = -1.05171, Holm p = 0.00524) were lower in the later ON session. The 178 s reanalysis preserved the same directions, although SR and especially MDT_path were more parameter-sensitive across sensitivity analyses. The fixed OFF-then-ON protocol was associated with reproducible within-subject differences in low-beta state dynamics, with the strongest evidence arising from SR and H. Because medication state was perfectly collinear with session order, these findings cannot distinguish medication-specific effects from order-, time-, vigilance-, fatigue-, or adaptation-related influences. FO_path and MDT_path remain conditional summaries tied to an internally defined OFF-dominant state, and MDT was less stable in the 178 s and OFF-only sensitivity analyses.

ai.topic: Dynamic EEG network-state analysis in Parkinson's
ai.reason: Uses source-space dynamic amplitude-envelope connectivity, switching rate, entropy, and dwell time; transferable state-space/dynamical-system and longitudinal modeling ideas for neural time-series.
ai.summary: In 39 Parkinson's disease patients with paired OFF/ON resting-state EEG, low-beta (13-20 Hz) dynamic amplitude-envelope connectivity showed higher switching rate and entropy in the later ON session compared to the earlier OFF session, with lower fractional occupancy and mean dwell time of an OFF-dominant state. The fixed OFF-then-ON protocol confounds medication state with session order, time, vigilance, fatigue, and adaptation, so medication-specific effects cannot be distinguished.

papers.title: Attenuated alpha state transitions and disrupted repetition-dependent temporal adaptation in mild cognitive impairment
papers.abstract: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) may involve impaired dynamic regulation of brain states that is not captured by conventional resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). We quantified occipital alpha (8-12 Hz) transitions during three repeated eye-opening/eye-closure cycles in 60 healthy controls (HC) and 77 participants with MCI. Eye-state events were refined from frontal ocular artifacts. Transition magnitude was measured by the log-transformed post-/pre-event energy ratio, and transition success by the expected direction of alpha change. For canonical transitions meeting prespecified fit-quality criteria, mono-exponential fitting yielded transition onset (t_onset) and the post-onset time constant (tau). MCI showed weaker alpha suppression during eye opening, weaker alpha enhancement during eye closure, and lower odds of transition success. No significant group difference in tau was detected within the canonical quality-controlled subset. In contrast, t_onset showed significant Group x Trial interactions in both conditions: HC developed later onset during eye opening and earlier onset during eye closure across repetitions, whereas MCI showed no comparable change. These findings suggest reduced alpha state-transition capacity and altered repetition-dependent temporal organization in MCI.

ai.reason: Quantifies alpha transition dynamics and adaptation across repeated events; relevant to state-space/time-series modeling and event-related spectral analysis, with moderate transfer to vigilance-state tracking.
ai.summary: In 77 participants with mild cognitive impairment and 60 healthy controls, occipital alpha (8-12 Hz) transitions during repeated eye-opening/eye-closure cycles were weaker and less successful in MCI, with no group difference in post-onset time constant. MCI showed absent repetition-dependent temporal adaptation: healthy controls developed later onset during eye opening and earlier onset during eye closure across trials, whereas MCI did not.

papers.title: Robust and replicable effects of ageing on resting-state brain electrophysiology measured with MEG.
papers.abstract: Non-invasive recordings of brain electrophysiology provide credible insights into decline in neuronal functioning with age. New approaches are required to translate these results into compelling clinical metrics and meet the global challenge of preserving brain health in ageing. Changes in neuronal dynamics with ageing are observable in the power spectra of EEG and MEG recordings. Highly promising candidates for electrophysiological markers have been identified, but progress is hindered by substantial methodological variability across studies. This makes it challenging to establish a clear consensus on the frequency, location, and direction of any single reported effect within the larger body of research. We estimate a full-frequency whole-head profile of the ageing effect on eyes-closed resting-state MEG using the GLM-Spectrum. This data representation is easily sharable, facilitates meta-analyses, and provides a framework for estimating statistical power of age effects for future study planning. We use this to show that the effect of age replicates across open-access MEG datasets and is robust to modelling of common covariates. Distinct components within the full-frequency profile have different effect sizes, indicating that sample-size planning for ageing effects must consider the specific features of interest. The frequency profile of ageing is strongly robust to a range of common covariates and partially robust to modelling of grey matter volume. We establish that what seems a well-powered study may become underpowered when analyses target an age effect that is linearly separable from an age-relevant covariate such as grey matter volume. These results provide a pathway towards formal comparison and assessment of candidate markers for brain health in ageing.

ai.topic: Robust MEG ageing effects with GLM-Spectrum
ai.reason: Introduces a sharable spectral representation (GLM-Spectrum) and replicable full-frequency electrophysiology analysis, transferable to spectral EEG methods.
ai.summary: Using the GLM-Spectrum on eyes-closed resting-state MEG, this study estimates a full-frequency whole-head profile of ageing effects that replicates across open-access datasets and is robust to common covariates. Distinct frequency components have different effect sizes, and the age effect is partially robust to grey matter volume modeling, showing that targeting an age effect linearly separable from a covariate can reduce statistical power.

papers.title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification
papers.abstract: Background: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly affect cognitive, academic, and social functioning. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive tool for identifying objective neurophysiological biomarkers of ADHD because of its high temporal resolution and cost-effectiveness, many existing machine learning studies rely on single-domain EEG features, which may not adequately capture the complex functional organization of the brain. Methods: This study proposes a subject-level EEG classification framework that integrates three complementary feature domains: spectral characteristics, weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI)-based functional connectivity, and topological descriptors derived from persistent homology. EEG recordings from 121 subjects were preprocessed and segmented into overlapping windows for feature extraction. Window-level features were aggregated to generate subject-level representations. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was employed to select the 110 most informative features from an initial set of 1,043 descriptors. Five machine learning classifiers, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. An ablation study was further conducted to assess the contribution of each feature domain. Model interpretability was investigated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), two widely adopted Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for interpreting machine learning models. Results: Among the evaluated classifiers, the SVM achieved the highest classification performance, yielding an accuracy of 80.17%, an F1-score of 80.95%, a balanced accuracy of 80.14%, a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 86.72%, and a precision recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 87.34%. The ablation study demonstrated that combining spectral, functional connectivity, and topological features consistently outperformed individual feature domains, highlighting the complementary nature of these representations. Explainable AI analyses further identified functional connectivity features as the primary contributors to classification performance while confirming the additional value of spectral and topological descriptors. Conclusions: The proposed framework demonstrates that integrating spectral analysis, functional connectivity, and topological data analysis provides an effective and interpretable approach for subject-level ADHD classification from EEG recordings. The combination of recursive feature selection, multi-domain feature fusion, ablation analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence establishes a transparent and reproducible pipeline that may facilitate the development of reliable EEG-based clinical decision-support systems for ADHD.

ai.topic: Multi-domain EEG feature engineering for classification
ai.reason: Integrates spectral, connectivity, and topological features with RFE for subject-level classification; transferable feature engineering ideas for sleep staging and vigilance-state classification.
ai.summary: The study developed an EEG classification framework for subject-level ADHD diagnosis by integrating spectral, functional connectivity (wPLI), and topological (persistent homology) features. Using SVM after recursive feature elimination, it achieved 80.17% accuracy and 86.72% ROC-AUC, with ablation showing multi-domain fusion outperformed single domains and explainable AI highlighting functional connectivity as the primary contributor.

papers.title: From Computational Models to Clinical Decision-Making in Epilepsy: Bridging the Gap Between Theory and Practice.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is one of the most heterogeneous and unpredictable neurological disorders, characterized by complex brain dynamics, significant interindividual variability, and a therapeutic response that is often difficult to predict. Despite major advances in neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and antiepileptic treatments, clinical decision-making still faces major challenges, including precisely localizing the epileptogenic zone, predicting seizures, identifying drug-resistant patients, and optimizing personalized therapeutic strategies. Over the past two decades, computational models have gradually emerged as promising tools for addressing these challenges. Early approaches relied primarily on mechanistic biophysical models aimed at reproducing the neural dynamics and mechanisms of hyperexcitability involved in epileptogenesis. More recently, the rise of artificial intelligence and deep learning has facilitated the development of predictive models capable of leveraging large-scale multimodal data. Finally, the emergence of digital brain twins and adaptive closed-loop systems now paves the way for personalized computational medicine integrating simulation, prediction, and real-time therapeutic intervention. This review provides a critical analysis of the major international initiatives developed between 2004 and 2026, including the EPICLUSTER/EBRAINS, EPINOSTICS, ENIGMA-Epilepsy, NeuroPace RNS, SeizeIT, EpiBioS4Rx, and NeuroVista projects, as well as several translational platforms based on artificial intelligence and biophysical modeling. We evaluate the actual contribution of these models to clinical decision-making in epilepsy, their translational contributions, their methodological limitations, and the challenges associated with their integration into hospital settings. We argue that the future of computational epileptology does not rest on the opposition between artificial intelligence and mechanistic models, but on their convergence within explainable, personalized, and clinically interpretable hybrid architectures.

ai.topic: Computational models for epilepsy clinical decisions
ai.reason: Review connecting computational models, AI, and clinical decision-making in epilepsy; adjacent background for dynamical modeling and clinical translation, but not a concrete transferable EEG analysis method.
ai.summary: This review critically analyzes major international computational epileptology initiatives from 2004 to 2026, covering mechanistic biophysical models, AI/deep-learning predictive models, and digital brain twin or adaptive closed-loop systems, and evaluates their actual contribution to clinical decision-making. It argues that future progress depends on hybrid, explainable architectures that converge AI with mechanistic modeling rather than treating them as opposing approaches.

papers.title: Intracranial characterization of gamma in humans in response to auditory gratings
papers.abstract: Activity in the gamma frequency range (>30Hz) serves as a neural hallmark of stimulus encoding across multiple sensory modalities. Based on its distinct properties, this activity could be classified as broadband or narrowband oscillations. Visual stimuli, such as a grating, induce narrowband oscillations, which have shown promise as diagnostic markers for neurological disorders. However, such tasks are discomforting for the subjects. These can be made subject-friendly by swapping the stimulus for an auditory one; however, most auditory stimuli elicit a broadband activity. In search of an ideal candidate to induce auditory narrowband oscillations, we previously recorded responses to auditory gratings in electroencephalography (EEG) recordings (Gulati & Ray, 2024) using a passive listening paradigm. We observed a focal sustained broadband increase in high gamma activity (70-150Hz), which was not selective towards any stimulus attributes. Nevertheless, since EEG represents activity of a large population, it remained unclear whether observed activity represented a broadband increase or comprised multiple narrowband rhythms, and whether it was indeed untuned. To elucidate this, we recorded invasively from the regions on and around the superior temporal gyrus, closer to Heschl's gyrus of seven patients undergoing epilepsy resection surgery. Patients were either under anesthesia or fully awake while we presented auditory gratings through loudspeakers. We found a transient increase in broadband gamma activity (30-100Hz) followed by a sustained suppression of beta rhythm (14-28Hz). This broadband gamma was selective for slower spectro-temporal modulations. Our result compares the responses obtained across different recording scales and corroborates that auditory gratings produce broadband but not narrowband gamma activity.

ai.reason: Human intracranial narrowband/broadband gamma characterization is relevant to spectral analysis of neural time-series, but its stimulus-specific auditory focus and intracranial setting are only adjacent to EEG/animal sleep methods.
ai.summary: Intracranial recordings in seven epilepsy patients during auditory grating presentation showed a transient broadband gamma increase (30-100 Hz) followed by sustained beta suppression (14-28 Hz), with gamma selective for slower spectro-temporal modulations.

papers.title: Modulation of the speed of Intrinsic Alpha Frequency (IAF) with tACS modulates variability of illusory speech perception
papers.abstract: Navigating the world requires our brains to constantly process a massive influx of information from the environment. One of the most remarkable yet complex feats the human brain performs daily is speech perception. It is a multifaceted, hierarchical process that relies heavily on the integration of auditory and visual cues, particularly in noisy environments. Neural integration of these streams is hypothesized to depend on temporal mechanisms governed by individual alpha frequency (IAF, 8-12 Hz), which serves as a key neural correlate of the temporal binding window (TBW). While IAF has been linked to multisensory integration, its role in shaping multisensory illusions remains largely unexplored. Here, we tested this directly using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to modulate occipital activity during multisensory conflict. In a two-day protocol involving 27 healthy participants, resting-state EEG was recorded to determine IAF. On Day 2, participants then performed a multisensory speech task involving congruent (pa/, /ta/, /ka/) and incongruent McGurk stimuli (auditory /pa/, visual /ka/), both at baseline and during tACS applied at IAF and offset frequencies (IAF +/- 2 Hz) over occipital electrodes. While accuracy for congruent syllables remained high across conditions, results revealed that tACS significantly reduced the perception of illusory /ta/ percepts during McGurk trials. Finally, using a phenomenological model based on Kuramoto oscillators, we provided a mechanistic explanation for the percentage of illusory responses observed across participants under the influence of tACS at IAF and offsets. This study highlights the potential for targeted neuromodulatory interventions to influence multisensory processing in clinical or professional settings.

ai.topic: tACS modulation of intrinsic alpha frequency and speech perception
ai.reason: Human EEG and alpha-frequency methods are adjacent, but focus on tACS and multisensory perception rather than sleep or transferable analysis tools.
ai.summary: Using tACS at intrinsic alpha frequency and ±2 Hz offsets over occipital electrodes in 27 healthy participants, this study found that tACS significantly reduced illusory /ta/ percepts in McGurk trials and that a Kuramoto-oscillator model explained the percentage of illusory responses.

papers.title: Brief Trains of Closed-loop TMS Induce Controllable Power in FM-theta Oscillations
papers.abstract: Objective. Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta; 4-8 Hz) oscillations are thought to support cognition. Brief trains of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can probe these oscillations with high temporal precision but have rarely changed theta power. One possible reason is that prior studies ignored the instantaneous phase of the oscillation, which strongly shapes the cortical response to TMS. We tested whether brief TMS trains triggered at specific FM-theta phases in real time directionally modulate post-train FM-theta power. Approach. Six healthy adults received TMS over dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Fz) with concurrent electroencephalography during a whole-report working memory task. A beamformer and real-time phase-estimation pipeline triggered four-pulse 6 Hz trains (110% of resting motor threshold) at FM-theta peaks (0 degrees) or troughs (180 degrees), randomized trial by trial. Post-train spectral power was decomposed into total, induced (non-phase-locked) and evoked (phase-locked) components. Main results. Trough-triggered trains transiently increased post-train FM-theta power relative to peak-triggered trains; task performance did not differ. Cluster-based permutation tests showed trough-peak differences in total (4.6-7.1 Hz) and induced (5.0-7.8 Hz) power ~50-440 ms after the train, suggesting amplification of the oscillation . No evoked effect was detected. The total-power effect was robust at the subject level (Cohen's dz = 1.32, p = 0.023). Within-train theta power did not differ between conditions, suggesting a cortical origin. Significance. To our knowledge, this is the first study to lock brief rhythmic TMS trains to the real-time phase of an ongoing oscillation, and to show phase-dependent modulation of FM-theta power after individual trains on timescales relevant to behavior. Open-loop brief-train protocols may have missed such effects by mixing faciliatory and suppressive phases. Phase-locked brief trains offer a precise tool for testing the causal role of oscillations in cognition.

ai.reason: Real-time phase estimation and spectral power decomposition are transferable signal-processing ideas, but TMS-driven human cognitive work is not central to animal sleep or lightweight EEG analysis.
ai.summary: This study locked brief rhythmic TMS trains to real-time frontal-midline theta phase in six healthy adults and found that trough-triggered, but not peak-triggered, trains transiently increased post-train FM-theta power (4.6-7.1 Hz) about 50-440 ms after stimulation, without affecting task performance.

papers.title: A touch that lingers: synchronized patting strengthens neural tracking of auditory rhythm in newborns
papers.abstract: Rhythmic auditory stimulation in early life rarely occurs in isolation. Caregivers naturally combine singing and speech with rhythmic touch, rocking, and visual cues. Newborns are sensitive to auditory rhythm from birth, yet little is known about how temporally aligned information across sensory modalities shapes the neural encoding of auditory rhythmic structure. Here, we tested whether rhythmic touch can alter how the newborn brain tracks an ongoing auditory signal beyond the period of tactile stimulation. We recorded high-density electroencephalography from full-term newborns (N = 40), 1-3 days after birth, while they were exposed to recorded French lullabies presented either alone or accompanied by gentle patting synchronized with the metrically strong beat. Patting was delivered intermittently, allowing us to compare neural responses to lullabies across conditions, notably during periods without concurrent tactile stimulation. We quantified neural tracking of the lullabies using brain-stimulus coherence and temporal response function modeling. Newborns' neural activity synchronized with the rhythmic structure of the lullabies at frequencies corresponding to both the beat and the metrically accented strong beat. Critically, neural tracking was stronger when the lullabies had been accompanied by synchronized touch than when they were presented alone, and this enhancement persisted during subsequent periods in which no touch was delivered. Although rhythmic touch enhanced tracking in newborns with both weaker and stronger auditory-only tracking, there was a larger gain in those who initially showed weaker auditory tracking. Together, our findings reveal that the newborn brain exploits rhythmic touch to strengthen its encoding of auditory rhythm, and that this benefit outlasts the touch itself. This provides neural evidence that patting an infant in time with a song, a caregiving practice shared across cultures, does more than simply provide a tactile stimulation. It shapes how the newborn brain encodes the song's rhythm.

ai.topic: Neural tracking of auditory rhythm in newborns
ai.reason: Uses EEG brain-stimulus coherence and temporal response functions; relevant signal-processing methods but developmental auditory focus.
ai.summary: In 40 full-term newborns, high-density EEG showed that neural tracking of French lullabies was stronger when songs were accompanied by synchronized patting, and this enhancement persisted during subsequent periods without touch, especially in newborns with weaker auditory-only tracking.

papers.title: Acoustic Context Shapes Cortical Encoding of Spectral Discrimination in Normal and Impaired Hearing
papers.abstract: The auditory change complex (ACC) provides a cortical measure of acoustic discrimination, yet the mechanisms shaping responses to spectrotemporally complex sounds remain poorly understood. We investigated how acoustic context and temporal-envelope variability influence cortical encoding of spectral contrast in normal-hearing (NH) and hearing-impaired (HI) listeners. Electroencephalography (EEG) was used to record ACCs and auditory steady-state responses (ASSRs) evoked by spectrotemporally modulated stimuli. We compared conventional spectro-temporal modulations (STMs) with a novel discrete spectro-temporal modulation (DSTM) paradigm, examined temporal roving, and evaluated cortical responses to spectral contrast in NH and HI listeners. ACCs elicited by DSTM stimuli were larger and more symmetrical across transition directions than those elicited by conventional STMs. Temporal roving markedly reduced responses to intensity changes while largely preserving responses to spectral changes, indicating a partial dissociation between intensity-driven and spectrally driven cortical discrimination. ACC responses decreased systematically with spectral contrast and were weaker and delayed in HI listeners. By contrast, ASSRs remained highly detectable and showed no systematic dependence on spectral contrast, supporting a distinction between contrast-sensitive cortical discrimination and ongoing envelope encoding. Temporal roving further enhanced separation between NH and HI listeners. ACC response strength was significantly associated with behavioural STM discrimination thresholds and explained variance beyond age and audiometric thresholds. These findings demonstrate that cortical representations of spectral discrimination are shaped by acoustic context and temporal-envelope statistics. Temporal roving attenuates intensity-driven responses while preserving spectrally driven discrimination, providing insight into cortical encoding of spectrotemporal contrast and its relationship to perceptual performance.

papers.title: Simultaneous recordings link intracranial and scalp correlates of somatosensory awareness in humans
papers.abstract: The electrophysiological events underlying the conscious perception of touch in humans remain elusive. Scalp-EEG studies have identified a negative deflection peaking 120-200 ms after stimulus onset, known as the N140. This component, recently reinterpreted as the somatosensory awareness negativity (N140/SAN), has been proposed as a putative marker of tactile awareness, but its underlying neuronal dynamics are still unknown. Intracranial studies have shown that responses to median nerve stimulation include, after an initial phasic activation mainly localized to primary somatosensory cortices, a predominantly insulo-opercular tonic broadband high-frequency activity (BHA; 50-150 Hz) that has been linked to tactile awareness. Yet these scalp and intracranial signatures have never been directly linked. Using simultaneous high-density scalp EEG and intracranial EEG recordings, we show that the N140/SAN is the scalp manifestation of the insulo-opercular local field potential that follows the BHA response to stimulation. By bridging invasive and non-invasive recordings our results identify the neural origins of the N140/SAN and connect scalp and intracranial correlates of somatosensory awareness.

The results identify the neural origins of the N140/SAN and connect scalp and intracranial correlates of somatosensory awareness.

papers.title: How aging reshapes implicit learning: behavioral and oscillatory evidence from an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm.
papers.abstract: Most of everyday memory formation occurs without deliberate intent, yet the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding and their reorganization with age remain poorly understood. The present study investigated age-related changes in implicit learning using an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm (the Disjunctive Inference Implicit Learning Test, DIILT) in 31 younger and 35 older adults, paired with a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment and a one-month delayed recognition measure. Behaviorally, younger adults rapidly acquired novel implicit associations across the learning phase, whereas older adults showed persistent reliance on familiar items and limited improvement for novel associations. Critically, both groups successfully retained novel associations after one month, with implicitly learned associations showing greater long-term stability than explicitly encoded ones regardless of age. At the neural level, younger adults exhibited early posterior theta engagement for novel compared to familiar items, which disappeared by the end of learning, consistent with novelty-driven associative encoding. Older adults showed no such theta modulation for novel items, pointing to reorganization of the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding. Theta dynamics predicted immediate recognition in younger adults but not in older adults who rather showed theta association with processing speed, suggesting an age-related shift from memory-specific binding to domain-general cognitive resource allocation, consistent with neural maintenance frameworks of cognitive aging. These findings demonstrate that implicit encoding produces durable memory traces across the lifespan but relies on reorganized oscillatory dynamics in aging, with implications for understanding how cognitive aging reshapes everyday memory formation.

papers.title: Advances in monitoring the injured brain.
papers.abstract: Multimodal neuromonitoring has emerged as a cornerstone of modern neurocritical care for traumatic brain injury (TBI). Traditional monitoring approaches based on intracranial pressure (ICP) and clinical examination alone have proven insufficient to capture the complex, heterogeneous pathophysiology that drives secondary brain injury. Over the past decade, significant advances in monitoring technology, including brain tissue oxygenation, cerebral microdialysis, continuous electroencephalography, near‑infrared spectroscopy, cerebrovascular autoregulation assessment and non‑invasive techniques have enabled clinicians to individualize treatment strategies based on real‑time physiological data. Concurrently, artificial intelligence and machine learning are transforming data integration and prognostic modelling, and non‑invasive and wearable approaches are beginning to extend brain monitoring beyond high‑resource neuro‑ICUs. This review examines recent innovations in neuromonitoring for TBI, highlighting invasive and non‑invasive modalities, their integration into multimodal platforms, and emerging technologies that promise to make precision neurocritical care a clinical reality. As we move toward the future of neurosurgery, the challenge lies not only in developing advanced monitoring tools but in interpreting them in the context of host‑specific factors and translating complex physiological signals into timely, evidence‑based interventions that improve patient outcomes.

It highlights integration into multimodal platforms and the role of artificial intelligence and machine learning in data integration and prognostic modeling for precision neurocritical care.

papers.title: Motor effort biases perceptual decisions through later-stage evidence accumulation rather than early sensory-attentional processing
papers.abstract: Motor effort has been shown to bias perceptual decisions toward less effortful choices, but it remains unknown whether this bias already takes effect during the early stages of decision formation through preparatory attentional allocation or sensory processing, or during later-stage evidence accumulation preceding response execution. This study investigated when motor effort becomes integrated into decision formation by focusing on the temporal evolution of neural processing during perceptual decision-making. While 64-channel EEG was recorded, twenty-four healthy adults performed an orientation discrimination task in which two Gabor patches appeared simultaneously in the left and right visual hemifield and decisions were reported using two pressure-sensitive response buttons requiring different levels of force. We found that motor effort modulated EEG activity at both the preparatory and later decision stages: pre-stimulus alpha power was reduced over the occipito-parietal cortex contralateral to the low-effort option, and mean centro-parietal positivity (CPP) amplitude preceding response execution was greater over centro-parietal cortex for low-effort choices, while leaving early sensory representations intact as indicated by no differences in P1 or N1 amplitude following stimulus onset. Trial-by-trial CPP amplitude preceding response execution increased with the likelihood of selecting the low-effort option, whereas the pre-stimulus alpha modulation was not associated with behavioral decision bias. These findings suggest that motor effort biases perceptual decisions primarily during later-stage evidence accumulation, thereby providing insight into the neural basis of embodied perceptual decision making.

Motor effort reduced pre-stimulus alpha power contralateral to the low-effort option and increased pre-response centro-parietal positivity for low-effort choices without altering early P1/N1 sensory responses, with trial-by-trial CPP amplitude predicting low-effort selection, indicating a later-stage evidence accumulation bias.

papers.title: A Novel Digital Phenotype of Physical Activity: Associations with Heart Rate Fragmentation
papers.abstract: Background Heart rate fragmentation (HRF) has emerged as a novel marker of sinoatrial instability and neuroautonomic dysregulation and is a predictor of incident cardiovascular disease (CVD) events and cardiovascular mortality. Leveraging heart rate fragmentation as a novel measure may help us better understand the prognostic significance of physical activity. Physical activity (PA) patterns are multidimensional and difficult to study holistically, however. We sought to examine for novel PA clusters in a cohort of veteran men and evaluate their prognostic significance based on their associations with neuroautonomic dysregulation. Methods In this cross-sectional study, we examined 602 male veterans from the Vietnam Era Twins Study of Electrophysiology in Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (VETS-EP) who were enrolled between 2022 and 2026. Accelerometry data were used to derive physical activity parameters across 6 domains: volume, sedentary behavior, intensity, diurnal pattern, fragmentation, and variability. Heart rate fragmentation was assessed using percentage of inflection points (PIP), inverse average length of segments (IALS), percentage of short segments (PSS), and percentage of alternating segments (PAS). Gaussian mixture models were used to derive digital phenotypes of physical activity, and associations with heart rate fragmentation were assessed using linear mixed models. Results Participants had a mean age of 73.8 {+/-} 2.9 years and 93.2% reported White race. Two overlapping phenotypes of physical activity patterns were identified: a compact-early phenotype, characterized by earlier activity timing and slightly greater overall activity, and a diffuse-late phenotype, characterized by later activity timing and greater heterogeneity in activity volume. In fully adjusted models, the diffuse-late phenotype was associated with higher PIP, the primary outcome ({beta}: 1.199, 95% CI: 0.034 to 2.363, p-value: 0.044), and higher IALS ({beta}: 0.01210, 95% CI: 0.00048 to 0.02373, p-value: 0.041), but not PSS or PAS, compared with the compact-early phenotype. Conclusions In older male veterans, Gaussian mixture model phenotyping identified two overlapping physical activity phenotypes, differing mainly in diurnal timing and in the dispersion of overall activity, that were associated with modest differences in heart rate fragmentation. These phenotypes provide a framework for capturing complex physical activity patterns. Future prospective studies representing diverse populations are needed to validate such phenotypes.

papers.title: How do Uncompensated Micro-Shifts Systematically Confound Low-Concentration Metabolite Quantification in 1H-MRS Analysis?
papers.abstract: Linear combination model fitting is widely used for spectral analysis in 1H-MRS but relies on basis sets with fixed spin-system parameters, implicitly neglecting the sensitivity of chemical shifts to physiological and pathological tissue microenvironments. This study systematically evaluated the impact of frequency perturbations on spectral analysis and reassessed the validity of the Cramér-Rao lower bounds (CRLB) as a quality-control metric for low-concentration metabolites. The effects of frequency perturbations on spectral analysis were investigated using simulated datasets with different baseline models and lineshapes, followed by validation in a publicly available in vivo human brain 1H-MRS dataset (n = 31). Estimated metabolite concentrations, relative concentration changes, estimation errors, and CRLB values were analyzed across all conditions. Frequency perturbations produced minimal quantification changes in high-concentration metabolites but substantially larger errors in several low-concentration metabolites. Across both simulations and in vivo validation, relative concentration changes generally remained below 3% for high-concentration metabolites but exceeded 10%-20% for several low-concentration metabolites, including Gln, GSH, Asp, and NAAG. Importantly, substantial estimation errors frequently occurred despite CRLB values remaining within conventionally acceptable ranges. These findings were consistently observed across different baseline models, lineshapes, and in vivo validation. Physiologically relevant frequency perturbations can introduce substantial quantification bias that is not consistently reflected by CRLB. These findings identify environmentally induced resonance-frequency variations as an underrecognized source of quantification error in current linear-combination model fitting and suggest that CRLB alone is insufficient for assessing quantification reliability, particularly under conditions associated with altered brain temperature or tissue pH.

papers.title: Large-scale all-optical electrophysiology links excitability and connectivity to circuit dynamics in vivo
papers.abstract: To understand neural computations, one would like to relate circuit dynamics to neuronal intrinsic excitability and connectivity. We developed tools for large-scale all-optical electrophysiology and applied them to approximately 300 layer 1 interneurons per mouse in vivo. Across two mice, targeted stimulation and voltage imaging identified 1,469 inhibitory and 5,752 directed electrical connections among 14,312 tested pairs. Presynaptic identity was more strongly associated with inhibitory post-synaptic potential (IPSP) amplitude, whereas postsynaptic identity was more strongly associated with IPSP decay time. Gap junctional and synaptic interactions had distinct spatiotemporal kernels, with corresponding signatures in spontaneous activity. Excitability measured under optogenetic stimulus predicted spiking responses to subthreshold voltage, depolarization rate, and spike history during spontaneous firing. Genetic subtypes also showed different behavioral-state-dependent voltage-to-spike relationships despite similar population-average subthreshold voltages. These measurements link cellular properties and pairwise interactions to spontaneous circuit dynamics, establishing an approach for functional circuit mapping in vivo.

papers.title: Effects of morning versus evening high-intensity exercise on electroencephalographic and autonomic responses in middle-aged women.
papers.abstract: The time of day at which exercise is performed influences physiological responses and performance, and thus its health benefits. This study investigated whether electroencephalographic (EEG) and autonomic nervous system responses to morning versus evening exercise differed in middle-aged women. Thirty women aged 50-60 years were randomly assigned to a morning or evening exercise group. Participants were asked to sleep for seven to eight hours before testing. The morning group exercised at 6:00 am and the evening group at 6:00 pm. EEG-derived indices included the theta-to-beta ratio (TBR) and spectral edge frequency at 90% (SEF-90). Photoplethysmography-derived autonomic indices comprised the HRV index and HRV-derived sympathetic-related and parasympathetic-related indices, measured at rest before and immediately after exercise. Data were analyzed using a two-way mixed-design analysis of variance. For significant interactions, simple effects and change-score analyses were performed. TBR and SEF-90 showed significant group × time interactions, with greater changes from pre- to post-exercise in the morning group. TBR increased and SEF-90 decreased following exercise in both groups, with greater changes in the morning group. The HRV index showed only a significant main effect of time. However, HRV-derived sympathetic-related and parasympathetic-related indices demonstrated significant group × time interactions, with greater autonomic responses in the morning group, as measured by change scores. EEG- and HRV-derived neurophysiological response patterns to high-intensity exercise may vary with exercise timing. Morning high-intensity exercise may elicit greater neurophysiological responses than evening exercise, highlighting the importance of exercise timing in training strategies and recovery.

papers.title: Effects of Transcranial Photobiomodulation on Motor Functions in Healthy Individuals: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveThis study investigated the effects of transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM) targeting the supplementary motor area (SMA) on motor performance and neural activity in healthy individuals.MethodsIn a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, 60 right-handed participants received active tPBM (850 nm, 60 mW/cm2, 36 J/cm2) or sham stimulation over the SMA for four consecutive days. Motor performance was assessed using a sequential finger-tapping task for both hands. Neural activity was evaluated using quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG) at rest.ResultsActive tPBM significantly improved non-dominant hand motor performance compared to sham, with reductions in reaction time and total movement time, and increased accuracy (all p < 0.001 after Bonferroni correction). qEEG showed significant increases in alpha and beta power at C3 and C4 electrodes in the active group (all p < 0.001 after correction). No significant changes were observed in the sham group.ConclusionThese findings suggest that short-term tPBM targeting the SMA can enhance motor performance, particularly of the non-dominant hand, and increase sensorimotor alpha and beta power in healthy young adults. Further research is needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms and potential clinical applications.

papers.title: Positive emotional synchrony and intimacy satisfaction: evidence from a multidimensional assessment.
papers.abstract: Emotional synchrony, as an expression of emotional coordination and coherence, is an important indicator of the quality of intimate relationships. However, few studies have systematically examined valence-related differences in emotional synchrony and their implications for relationship satisfaction, and multidimensional evidence remains limited. In the present research, we employed a multidimensional assessment approach that combined behavioural coding, self-reports, and electroencephalography (EEG) hyperscanning to examine the predictive role of emotional synchrony in relationship satisfaction and the mediating role of self-other overlap during actual interactions. Study 1 revealed that positive emotions played a dominant role in emotional synchrony and directly and positively predicted males' intimacy satisfaction, with self-other overlap serving as a partial mediator. Using self-reports and EEG, Study 2 revealed that emotional synchrony/interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) directly and positively predicted intimacy satisfaction in men, whereas its effect on women's intimacy satisfaction was fully mediated by self-other overlap. In summary, positive emotional synchrony positively predicts intimacy satisfaction, which provides empirical support for the understanding of the behavioural and neural mechanisms underlying emotional synchrony.

papers.title: Micro and nanoscale probes for spatiotemporal cell analysis and manipulation.
papers.abstract: Understanding dynamic cellular processes requires technologies capable of probing living cells with high spatial and temporal precision while preserving viability. Conventional approaches, including bulk omics, microinjection, and electroporation, often provide only static snapshots or induce significant cellular perturbation. Recent advances in micro- and nanoscale probes are enabling minimally invasive intracellular delivery, sampling, sensing, and manipulation with unprecedented precision. This review examines the current state of the art in micro and nanoscale probe technologies, including fluidic force microscopy (FluidFM), nanopipettes, open-space microfluidic probes, and nanoneedle arrays. We discuss how these complementary platforms enable controlled delivery of biomolecules, longitudinal molecular sampling, intracellular electrophysiology, electrochemical sensing, and spatiotemporally resolved analyses from single cells to living tissues. We placed particular emphasis on their ability to overcome the limitations of destructive endpoint assays by facilitating repeated interrogation of the same cell, quantitative molecular delivery, and multimodal measurements with subcellular resolution. Finally, we discuss the remaining engineering challenges, including improving throughput, integrating complementary sensing modalities, and advancing these promising technologies into robust platforms for laboratory studies of cultured cells and tissues.

papers.title: Information avant la lettre: The mathematical constitution of brain waves in early EEG analysis (1929-1932).
papers.abstract: This article examines the epistemological conditions under which the brain's electrophysiological trace was first constituted as a mathematical object of analysis. Rather than treating information as a cultural metaphor externally projected onto the brain, the paper reconstructs how specific tools of signal analysis made the trace into an object that the informational lineage would come to require. Hans Berger's research of 1929-1931 secured the trace as an effect of nervous processes in the brain, but read it as the signal of a single source. The case study is Günther Dietsch's 1932 paper, the first application of Fourier analysis to the EEG signal. The article shows that spectral decomposition did not merely describe the signal but constituted it as a decomposable causal object, resolving a single continuous curve into a discrete set of components, each varying independently of the rest. No improvement of the recording apparatus could achieve this; only the mathematical intervention could. The case is read through the causal-deflationary theory of information in López and Lombardi (2019), according to which a source informs a destination only when a variable of the destination can be manipulated by the source. What 1932 builds is the object of a theory of information needs, not yet the measure that such a theory would later compute on it. That is what avant la lettre means here: mathematics made the trace informational before the theory existed.

papers.title: Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation in pediatric epileptic syndromes: mechanisms, limitations, and future research horizons.
papers.abstract: Drug-resistant epilepsy affects approximately 20 to 30% of children with epilepsy, with particularly devastating outcomes in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs). Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation (c-tDCS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive neuromodulation approach warranting systematic evaluation. Recent meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials demonstrate significant reductions in seizure frequency following c-tDCS compared with sham stimulation, corresponding to roughly 3 to 4 fewer seizures per month or a proportional reduction of about 45% at 4 weeks. Evidence supports efficacy in focal epilepsies and selected syndromes, including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and early-onset epileptic encephalopathies. Standard protocols employ 1 to 2 mA cathodal stimulation for 20 minutes over 5 to 10 consecutive sessions. High-definition tDCS configurations allow more focal current delivery. However, significant inter-individual variability exists, and the relationship between interictal epileptiform discharge suppression and clinical seizure outcomes remains inconsistent. Computational modeling demonstrates substantially higher cortical electric field strengths in children than in adults at equivalent current intensities, raising important dosing considerations. Safety data from over 600 pediatric sessions indicate favorable tolerability with no serious adverse events, although seizure exacerbation has been reported in a minority of participants in open-label studies. Cathodal tDCS represents a safe, tolerable, and potentially effective adjunct to unchanged antiseizure medication regimens in children with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and should presently be regarded as investigational. Selection criteria, optimal stimulation parameters, and syndrome-specific protocols require further refinement. Particular caution is warranted with transcranial alternating current stimulation in generalized epilepsies. Research priorities include closed-loop electroencephalography (EEG)-triggered stimulation systems, biomarker- driven patient selection, age-appropriate dosimetry informed by computational modeling, and adequately powered trials in specific DEE populations including West syndrome, Dravet syndrome, and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation during sleep.

papers.title: Pediatric Headache: A Practical Approach to Clinical Diagnosis and Management.
papers.abstract: Headache is among the most common neurological complaints of childhood and adolescence and can substantially impair school attendance and quality of life. A practical approach to the child with headache rests on four tasks: recognizing the primary headache phenotype, screening for the minority of children whose headache is secondary to another disorder, assessing how much the headache is disabling the child, and matching treatment intensity to that disability. Migraine and tension-type headache account for most primary headache presentations, but the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias and, rarely, painful cranial neuropathies must also be recognized because their management differs fundamentally from that of migraine. Diagnosis is clinical, based on a structured history, assessment of disability, and a careful general and neurological examination; red flags should prompt reassessment and risk stratification rather than reflexive neuroimaging, and in a child with a typical primary headache phenotype and a normal examination, routine imaging, laboratory testing, or electroencephalography is generally unnecessary. Management is multimodal: education and lifestyle measures form the foundation of care; acute treatment uses evidence-based, age-appropriate analgesics and triptans; and preventive treatment is reserved for children with substantial headache-related disability, bearing in mind the unusually high placebo response documented in pediatric migraine prevention trials. Several calcitonin gene-related peptide-targeted and device-based therapies have emerged for pediatric migraine since 2024, though pediatric evidence and regulatory status vary substantially by therapy. Tension-type headache and the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias require separate diagnostic and therapeutic consideration, and treatment of the latter reflects evidence largely extrapolated from adults and case series, rather than controlled pediatric trials. This review provides a practical, evidence-based framework for the clinical diagnosis and management of pediatric headache for the general clinician.

papers.title: Astrocyte SMN Restoration and Forskolin Treatment Improve SMA Synaptic Pathology.
papers.abstract: Early phenotypic presentation of central afferent synapse dysfunction within patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) represents a key target for therapeutic development; however, the underlying disease mechanisms remain unresolved. By further investigating motor neuron synapse and peri-synaptic astrocyte process (PAP) defects in human SMA disease pathology, we aimed to develop a novel therapeutic approach to improve motor neuron function. We utilized healthy subjects and patients with SMA induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cultures to assess phenotypes occurring intrinsically within astrocyte processes (monocultures) and at the PAP-synaptic interface (co-cultures), respectively, using cell surface capture mass spectrometry proteomics, confocal and super resolution microscopy, synaptogliosome (SG) isolation, and electrophysiology. SMA astrocytes demonstrated intrinsic filopodia actin defects featuring low abundance of actin-associated cell surface N-glycoproteins, decreased filopodia density and CDC42-GTP levels after actin remodeling stimulation, and significantly reduced phosphorylated ezrin, radixin, and moesin (pERM) proteins. Within the SMA motor neuron and astrocyte co-cultures, we observed concurrent decreases in synapse number, actin-associated synapsin I expression, and PAP-associated expression of pERM proteins. Our dual treatment paradigm using SMN1 gene therapy combined with forskolin treatment to stimulate actin dynamics via increasing cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels resulted in increased branching and filopodia density of SMA astrocytes, and improved synapse formation and function of SMA motor neurons. We define actin-associated defects impacting astrocyte filopodia dynamics and motor neuron synaptic function in SMA. This shaped our therapeutic approach targeted to SMN-dependent and actin-related disease mechanisms, which overall demonstrated improvements in motor neuron function and disease pathology. papers.title: 5-HT1A Antagonist WAY-100635 Prevents Chronic Neurodegeneration and Immune Activation After TBI
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) initiates secondary neurodegeneration that compromises interconnected neural circuits and contributes to persistent visual and neurobehavioral impairment. Pharmacological strategies that preserve vulnerable neurons and synapses while limiting chronic neuroinflammation remain an unmet therapeutic need. We previously identified the serotonin 1A receptor (5-HT1A) antagonist WAY-100635 through screening human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and demonstrated that it promotes neuroprotection through cyclic adenosine monophosphate-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis. Here, we investigated whether post-injury treatment extends this neuroprotective efficacy to cerebral and visual circuitry following TBI. Male C57BL/6J mice aged 2-3 months underwent unilateral controlled cortical impact (CCI) involving the left visual cortex. Mice were randomly assigned to sham, untreated injury or treated injury groups, with 3-10 sham controls and 5-8 mice per injury group across experiments. WAY-100635 was administered intraperitoneally at 5 mg/kg daily, beginning 1 hour after injury and continuing for 6 weeks. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed using motor and psychological-health-relevant risk-taking/behavioral disinhibition by elevated-plus-maze assessment, visual electrophysiology, optokinetic responses, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging, and retinal and cortical histopathology. Unilateral cortical injury produced bilateral RGC dysfunction and loss, with greater degeneration in the eye contralateral to the injured hemisphere, consistent with predominantly crossed murine visual projections. WAY-100635 significantly preserved RGC survival and function, improved visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, and preserved visually evoked cortical responses to contralateral eye stimulation. Diffusion MRI revealed bilateral visual pathway abnormalities, with treatment selectively normalizing fractional anisotropy and radial kurtosis in the optic tract ipsilateral to cortical injury. In perilesional cortex, treatment preserved neuronal cell bodies and synapses detected by synaptophysin immunoreactivity while markedly reducing microglial/macrophage activation and reactive astrogliosis. These effects were accompanied by improved early motor performance and attenuation of injury-associated increases in open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze. Cortical cavity volume was not significantly reduced, supporting preferential protection of vulnerable circuitry surrounding and connected to the primary lesion. These findings identify post-injury WAY-100635 treatment as a novel therapeutic intervention that combines neuronal and synaptic preservation with reduced chronic glial activation and improved functional outcomes. They support further translational development of serotonin 1A receptor antagonism to limit secondary neurodegeneration and the visual and neurobehavioral consequences of TBI.

papers.title: Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy Aptasensors for Nucleic-Acid Detection: Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Nucleic-acid biomarkers play pivotal roles in disease diagnosis, therapeutic monitoring, and precision medicine, creating an urgent demand for analytical platforms combining high sensitivity, molecular specificity, and rapid detection. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) integrated with aptamers, short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides, has attracted considerable attention by coupling programmable molecular recognition with ultrasensitive plasmon-enhanced Raman detection. This review evaluates recent advances in aptamer-based SERS biosensors for nucleic-acid analysis, systematically examining sensing mechanisms, plasmonic substrate engineering, aptamer immobilization, signal-transduction pathways, and amplification approaches, including catalytic hairpin assembly, hybridization chain reaction, rolling circle amplification, and CRISPR-assisted systems. Recent developments in microfluidics, artificial intelligence-assisted spectral analysis, portable Raman instrumentation, and point-of-care platforms are assessed while distinguishing true aptamer-mediated sensing from conventional hybridization-based DNA detection. Rational hotspot engineering, deterministic nanogap architectures, and advanced amplification strategies have enabled detection from femtomolar to attomolar levels with improved selectivity, multiplexing, and reproducibility. Challenges including substrate variability, quantitative standardization, aptamer stability, biosafety, and clinical translation are discussed. Future directions toward standardized, intelligent, clinically deployable SERS platforms for next-generation molecular diagnostics and precision healthcare are proposed.

papers.title: Step-by-Step Protocol for Fluorescence-Based Analysis of Uptake in Transporter-Expressing Xenopus laevis Oocytes.
papers.abstract: Xenopus laevis oocytes are widely used as a heterologous expression system for investigating the function of membrane proteins due to robust expression of heterologous protein and a low endogenous transport background. Traditionally, transporter activity in oocytes has been assessed using electrophysiology or radiolabeled uptake assays, approaches that are constrained by the requirement for electrogenicity of the transport process, availability of radiolabeled compounds, and instrumentation. Here, we describe a fluorescence-based uptake assay that enables direct and rapid quantification of transporter activity using a fluorescence plate reader. The protocol uses the Arabidopsis thaliana sucrose transporter 1 (SUC1) and its fluorescent substrate esculin as a case for how to set up the assay. The workflow includes optimizing assay conditions, sample preparation, fluorescent measurements, and downstream data analysis using R. This method can readily be adapted to other transporter-substrate pairs, and it supports applications such as transporter inhibitor screening, mutational analysis, characterization of kinetic properties, or indirect substrate specificity testing through competition assays. Overall, this protocol provides a simple and scalable alternative to traditional techniques, eliminating the need for radiolabeled compounds or electrophysiology while enabling easy quantitative assessment of transporter activity. Key features • Provides a simple, plate reader-based fluorescence uptake assay for quantifying transporter activity in Xenopus laevis oocytes. • Adaptable to any transporter with a compatible fluorescent substrate, supporting rapid testing of substrate specificity indirectly through competition assays or mutant screening. • Includes a complete workflow from assay setup and conduction to data analysis, suitable for both initial characterization and routine functional testing of membrane transporters.
